_link.title: I can recognise DNA replication as a necessary precursor to cell division

toLevel2.question: During which phase of the cell cycle does DNA replication occur?

options.text: S phase
options.explanation: DNA replication occurs during S (synthesis) phase of interphase, before the cell enters mitosis.

options.text: M phase
options.explanation: M phase is mitosis, when the cell divides. DNA replication must be completed before M phase begins.

options.text: G1 phase
options.explanation: G1 is a growth phase before S phase; DNA replication has not yet occurred during G1.

options.text: C phase
options.explanation: C phase is cytokinesis, the splitting of the cytoplasm after mitosis, not when DNA is replicated.

toLevel2.question: Why must DNA replication occur before a cell can divide?

options.text: So each daughter cell receives a complete copy of the genome
options.explanation: Replication ensures both daughter cells get a full, identical set of DNA after division.

options.text: So the cell can produce more mitochondria for energy needs
options.explanation: Mitochondrial production is separate from DNA replication in the nucleus.

options.text: So the cell membrane becomes more flexible for division
options.explanation: Membrane flexibility is not related to DNA replication; replication copies the genome.

options.text: So the cell can increase its overall size before dividing
options.explanation: Cell growth occurs during G1 and G2; DNA replication copies the genetic material.

toLevel2.question: What happens to the amount of DNA in a cell during S phase?

options.text: It doubles
options.explanation: During S phase, all DNA is replicated, so the total amount of DNA in the cell doubles.

options.text: It halves
options.explanation: DNA halving occurs during meiosis, not during S phase. S phase doubles the DNA content.

options.text: It stays the same
options.explanation: DNA content increases during S phase because each molecule is copied to produce two identical copies.

options.text: It triples
options.explanation: DNA is replicated once during S phase, producing a doubling, not a tripling, of DNA content.

toLevel2.question: If a cell has 9 picograms of DNA after cytokinesis, how much DNA will it contain at the end of S phase?

options.text: 18 picograms
options.explanation: DNA replication doubles the DNA content, so 9 picograms becomes 18 picograms after S phase.

options.text: 27 picograms
options.explanation: DNA is doubled, not tripled, during S phase. The correct amount is 18 picograms.

options.text: 9 picograms
options.explanation: The DNA content doubles during S phase, so it would increase from 9 to 18 picograms.

options.text: 4.5 picograms
options.explanation: DNA is doubled during S phase, not halved. Halving occurs during meiosis.

toLevel2.question: What would happen to daughter cells if DNA replication did not occur before cell division?

options.text: Each daughter cell would receive only half the required DNA
options.explanation: Without replication, the original DNA would be split, leaving each daughter cell with an incomplete genome.

options.text: Each daughter cell would receive double the required DNA
options.explanation: Without replication, there is less DNA available, not more, so cells would be deficient.

options.text: Each daughter cell would receive exactly the right amount
options.explanation: Without replication, the DNA cannot be evenly distributed as complete copies to both cells.

options.text: Each daughter cell would receive no DNA at all from division
options.explanation: Some DNA would still be present, but each cell would receive only half, not none.

toLevel2.question: DNA replication must occur during S phase before the cell can enter mitosis.

options.text: True
options.explanation: Correct. DNA replication in S phase ensures each daughter cell will receive a complete copy of the genome during mitosis.

options.text: False
options.explanation: This statement is true. S phase replication is a necessary precursor to mitosis.

toLevel2.question: After DNA replication, a cell contains the same amount of DNA as before replication.

options.text: True
options.explanation: After replication, the DNA content has doubled. A cell that started with 9 picograms would have 18 picograms.

options.text: False
options.explanation: Correct. DNA replication doubles the amount of DNA in the cell, so the content increases.

toLevel2.question: DNA replication occurs during {{blank:1}} phase, which must happen before {{blank:2}} phase.

options.text: S
options.explanation: S (synthesis) phase is when DNA replication takes place.

options.text: M
options.explanation: M phase is mitosis; DNA replication occurs earlier during S phase.

options.text: G1
options.explanation: G1 is a growth phase; DNA replication occurs in S phase which follows G1.

options.text: M
options.explanation: M phase (mitosis) requires that DNA has already been replicated in S phase.

options.text: G1
options.explanation: G1 occurs before S phase, not after it. M phase follows replication.

options.text: S
options.explanation: S phase is when replication occurs; the phase that follows and requires it is M phase.

toLevel2.question: Without DNA replication, each daughter cell would receive only {{blank:1}} the required DNA and would not be {{blank:2}}.

options.text: half
options.explanation: Without replication, the single copy of DNA would be split, giving each cell only half.

options.text: double
options.explanation: Without replication, cells receive less DNA, not more. Each gets only half.

options.text: all of
options.explanation: Without replication, there is only one copy to split, so each cell gets only half.

options.text: viable
options.explanation: Cells with only half the genome lack essential genes and cannot function, making them non-viable.

options.text: visible
options.explanation: The issue is viability (ability to survive), not visibility.

options.text: mobile
options.explanation: The issue is viability (ability to survive and function), not mobility.

toLevel2.question: DNA replication ensures each daughter cell receives a {{blank:1}}, identical copy of the {{blank:2}}.

options.text: complete
options.explanation: Replication produces a full copy so each daughter cell gets a complete set of DNA.

options.text: partial
options.explanation: Replication produces a complete copy, not a partial one.

options.text: random
options.explanation: Replication is precise, producing a complete and identical copy, not a random one.

options.text: genome
options.explanation: The genome is the complete set of DNA; replication copies the entire genome.

options.text: membrane
options.explanation: DNA replication copies the genome, not the cell membrane.

options.text: cytoplasm
options.explanation: DNA replication copies the genome, not the cytoplasm.

toLevel3.question: Why must S phase be completed before M phase can begin?

options.text: Each daughter cell needs a full genome, which requires prior replication
options.explanation: Without a doubled DNA content from S phase, mitosis would produce cells with incomplete genomes.

options.text: S phase produces the energy needed to power the mitotic spindle
options.explanation: S phase is for DNA synthesis, not energy production. Energy comes from cellular respiration.

options.text: M phase cannot physically occur until the cell membrane thickens
options.explanation: Membrane changes are not the reason S phase precedes M phase; genome duplication is the key reason.

options.text: S phase removes damaged organelles that would interfere with division
options.explanation: S phase replicates DNA; organelle recycling is a separate process unrelated to S phase.

toLevel3.question: How does the G2 checkpoint relate to DNA replication?

options.text: It verifies that DNA replication was completed accurately before mitosis
options.explanation: The G2 checkpoint checks for replication errors and completeness, ensuring the cell is ready for division.

options.text: It triggers the start of DNA replication within the nucleus
options.explanation: DNA replication occurs during S phase, not at the G2 checkpoint. G2 checks replication accuracy.

options.text: It breaks down unreplicated DNA to prevent errors in division
options.explanation: The G2 checkpoint does not destroy DNA; it checks for replication accuracy and completeness.

options.text: It has no connection to DNA replication or the S phase at all
options.explanation: The G2 checkpoint directly relates to S phase because it verifies replication accuracy.

toLevel3.question: What is the relationship between DNA content and the number of cells produced by mitotic divisions?

options.text: Each division doubles the cell number while maintaining DNA content per cell
options.explanation: Mitosis produces two identical cells with the same DNA content as the parent, so cell number doubles each division.

options.text: Each division halves the DNA content within every daughter cell produced
options.explanation: Mitosis maintains DNA content; meiosis halves it. Each mitotic daughter cell has the same DNA as the parent.

options.text: DNA content increases with each successive round of mitotic division
options.explanation: DNA content per cell stays constant through mitosis; only total cell number increases.

options.text: Cell number stays constant while DNA content doubles each division
options.explanation: Cell number doubles with each division; DNA content per cell remains the same.

toLevel3.question: Why is the production of identical DNA copies important for maintaining an organism's genetic integrity?

options.text: It ensures all body cells carry the same genetic information for consistent function
options.explanation: Identical replication means every cell in the body has the same genome, allowing coordinated and consistent function.

options.text: It allows each cell to develop a unique set of genes for its specific role
options.explanation: All body cells receive identical DNA; specialisation comes from gene expression, not different genomes.

options.text: It prevents the cell from ever needing to divide again after one replication
options.explanation: Cells can divide many times; each division requires a new round of replication.

options.text: It creates genetic variation that helps the organism adapt to change
options.explanation: Mitotic replication produces identical copies; genetic variation comes from meiosis and mutation.

toLevel3.question: If a single skin cell undergoes four mitotic divisions, how many daughter cells are produced and why?

options.text: 16 cells, because each division doubles the number of cells (2 to the power of 4)
options.explanation: Each mitotic division doubles the cell count: 1 becomes 2, then 4, 8, and finally 16 after four divisions.

options.text: 8 cells, because each division adds two cells to the existing total number
options.explanation: Each division doubles, not adds two. After four divisions: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 cells.

options.text: 4 cells, because one new cell is produced per division from the original
options.explanation: Each division doubles all existing cells, not just the original. The result is 16 cells.

options.text: 32 cells, because each division triples the number of cells that exist
options.explanation: Mitosis doubles the cell number each time. Four doublings from 1 gives 16, not 32.

toLevel3.question: How does the concept of DNA replication connect DNA structure to the cell cycle?

options.text: The double-stranded structure of DNA allows each strand to serve as a template during S phase
options.explanation: The complementary base-paired structure of DNA enables semi-conservative replication during S phase.

options.text: DNA structure is unrelated to the cell cycle and replication occurs independently
options.explanation: DNA structure directly enables replication; the double helix provides templates for copying.

options.text: The cell cycle determines the structure of DNA rather than the other way around
options.explanation: DNA structure enables replication within the cell cycle; the cycle does not change DNA structure.

options.text: DNA replication alters the base sequence to prepare for the next cell division
options.explanation: Replication produces identical copies; it does not alter the base sequence.

toLevel3.question: The G2 checkpoint verifies that DNA replication has been completed accurately before the cell proceeds to mitosis.

options.text: True
options.explanation: Correct. The G2 checkpoint checks for replication completeness and accuracy, preventing errors from being passed to daughter cells.

options.text: False
options.explanation: This statement is true. The G2 checkpoint is specifically responsible for checking replication accuracy before mitosis.

toLevel3.question: DNA replication connects DNA structure to the cell cycle because the {{blank:1}} nature of DNA allows each strand to act as a {{blank:2}} for copying.

options.text: double-stranded
options.explanation: The double-stranded structure means each strand can serve as a template during replication.

options.text: single-stranded
options.explanation: DNA is double-stranded, which is what allows semi-conservative replication.

options.text: triple-stranded
options.explanation: DNA is double-stranded, not triple-stranded.

options.text: template
options.explanation: Each strand serves as a template, guiding the synthesis of a new complementary strand.

options.text: barrier
options.explanation: Strands act as templates for replication, not as barriers.

options.text: nutrient
options.explanation: DNA strands serve as templates for copying, not as nutrients.

toLevel3.question: After four mitotic divisions, a single cell produces {{blank:1}} daughter cells because each division {{blank:2}} the cell number.

options.explanation: 2 to the power of 4 equals 16. Each division doubles the number of cells.
8 would be the result of three divisions (2 to the power of 3), not four.
4 would be the result of two divisions (2 to the power of 2), not four.

options.text: doubles
options.explanation: Mitosis produces two daughter cells from one parent, doubling the total each time.

options.text: triples
options.explanation: Mitosis produces two cells, not three, so it doubles rather than triples the number.

options.text: halves
options.explanation: Mitosis doubles the cell count; it does not reduce it.

toLevel3.question: The G2 checkpoint ensures replication was {{blank:1}} before the cell proceeds to {{blank:2}}.

options.text: accurate
options.explanation: The G2 checkpoint checks that DNA replication was completed without errors.

options.text: skipped
options.explanation: The G2 checkpoint verifies accuracy, not that replication was skipped.

options.text: reversed
options.explanation: The checkpoint confirms accurate replication, not reversal of the process.

options.text: mitosis
options.explanation: After passing the G2 checkpoint, the cell enters M phase (mitosis).

options.text: S phase
options.explanation: S phase occurs before G2; after the G2 checkpoint, the cell enters mitosis.

options.text: G1 phase
options.explanation: G1 comes before S phase. The G2 checkpoint leads into mitosis.

toLevel4.question: A scientist measures 6 picograms of DNA in a cell at the end of G1. What DNA content would they expect at the end of S phase?

options.text: 12 picograms
options.explanation: DNA replication during S phase doubles the DNA content, so 6 picograms becomes 12 picograms.

options.text: 6 picograms
options.explanation: DNA content doubles during S phase due to replication, so it would not remain at 6 picograms.

options.text: 3 picograms
options.explanation: DNA content doubles during S phase, not halves. Halving occurs during meiosis.

options.text: 24 picograms
options.explanation: DNA doubles once during S phase, from 6 to 12 picograms, not quadruples.

toLevel4.question: A drug blocks DNA replication. What effect would this have on a dividing cell population?

options.text: Cells would be arrested before mitosis because they cannot complete S phase
options.explanation: Without replication, the G2 checkpoint would prevent entry into mitosis, halting division.

options.text: Cells would continue dividing normally without any change to the process
options.explanation: Without DNA replication, cells cannot produce daughter cells with complete genomes.

options.text: Cells would divide faster because they skip the replication step entirely
options.explanation: Skipping replication would halt division at checkpoints, not speed it up.

options.text: Cells would immediately undergo apoptosis before reaching the S phase
options.explanation: The drug blocks replication during S phase; cells would arrest at G2, not die before S phase.

toLevel4.question: A cell line has a mutation that disables the G2 checkpoint. What consequence would this have for DNA replication errors?

options.text: Errors from replication would pass unchecked into daughter cells during mitosis
options.explanation: Without the G2 checkpoint, cells with replication errors would enter mitosis and pass those errors to daughter cells.

options.text: Replication errors would be corrected automatically without checkpoint involvement
options.explanation: The G2 checkpoint is a key mechanism for detecting errors; without it, errors go undetected.

options.text: The cell would be unable to replicate DNA at all during the S phase process
options.explanation: The G2 checkpoint occurs after S phase; its absence does not prevent replication itself.

options.text: The mutation would have no effect because other checkpoints handle all errors
options.explanation: While other checkpoints exist, the G2 checkpoint specifically checks replication accuracy.

toLevel4.question: A researcher observes a cell with double the normal DNA content but no signs of division. Which phase is this cell most likely in?

options.text: G2 phase, after replication but before mitosis has begun
options.explanation: In G2, DNA has been replicated (doubled) but the cell has not yet entered mitosis.

options.text: G1 phase, before any DNA replication has taken place
options.explanation: In G1, DNA has not been replicated, so the content would be at the normal level.

options.text: M phase, during active chromosome separation in the cell
options.explanation: During M phase, visible signs of division (chromosome condensation, spindle formation) would be apparent.

options.text: G0 phase, where the cell has permanently exited the cycle
options.explanation: G0 cells have not replicated their DNA and would have normal DNA content.

toLevel4.question: In a tissue culture, cells are treated with a substance that prevents DNA polymerase from functioning. What would be observed?

options.text: Cells would accumulate in S phase, unable to complete replication
options.explanation: DNA polymerase is essential for replication. Without it, cells cannot complete S phase and would stall there.

options.text: Cells would proceed through mitosis faster than untreated cells
options.explanation: Without DNA polymerase, replication cannot occur, so cells cannot progress past S phase.

options.text: Cells would skip S phase and enter mitosis with unreplicated DNA
options.explanation: Checkpoints prevent cells from entering mitosis without completing replication.

options.text: Cells would not be affected because DNA polymerase is not needed
options.explanation: DNA polymerase is essential for DNA replication; its inhibition prevents S phase completion.

toLevel4.question: A bone marrow sample contains cells at various stages. Which measurement would distinguish cells in G1 from cells in G2?

options.text: DNA content, because G2 cells have double the DNA of G1 cells
options.explanation: G1 cells have not replicated (normal DNA), while G2 cells have completed S phase (doubled DNA).

options.text: Cell size, because G1 cells are always larger than G2 cells
options.explanation: While size changes occur, DNA content is the definitive way to distinguish G1 from G2.

options.text: Protein levels, because G2 cells contain no proteins at all
options.explanation: Both G1 and G2 cells contain proteins; DNA content is the key distinguishing measurement.

options.text: Lipid concentration, because G1 cells have more lipids than G2
options.explanation: Lipid content does not reliably distinguish cell cycle phases; DNA content does.

toLevel4.question: If a cell with 10 picograms of DNA undergoes one complete cell cycle, what DNA content would each daughter cell have?

options.text: 10 picograms, the same as the original parent cell
options.explanation: DNA doubles to 20 picograms in S phase, then is split equally during mitosis, giving each daughter cell 10 picograms.

options.text: 20 picograms, double the amount of the parent cell
options.explanation: DNA doubles during S phase but is then divided equally during mitosis, returning to 10 picograms per cell.

options.text: 5 picograms, half the amount of the original parent cell
options.explanation: DNA halving occurs in meiosis, not mitosis. Mitotic daughter cells have the same DNA as the parent.

options.text: 15 picograms, one and a half times the parent amount
options.explanation: DNA doubles then divides equally; each daughter cell receives the same amount as the parent.

toLevel4.question: A drug that blocks DNA polymerase would prevent cells from completing {{blank:1}} phase, causing them to {{blank:2}} before mitosis.

options.text: S
options.explanation: DNA polymerase is needed for replication in S phase; blocking it stalls cells there.

options.text: M
options.explanation: DNA polymerase acts during S phase, not M phase.

options.text: G1
options.explanation: DNA polymerase is active during S phase for replication, not during G1.

options.text: arrest
options.explanation: Cells unable to complete replication are arrested by checkpoints and cannot proceed to mitosis.

options.text: divide
options.explanation: Cells cannot divide without completing replication; they would arrest instead.

options.text: shrink
options.explanation: Cells do not shrink when replication is blocked; they arrest at the checkpoint.

toLevel4.question: A cell with 8 picograms of DNA in G1 would have {{blank:1}} picograms at the end of S phase and {{blank:2}} picograms in each daughter cell after mitosis.

options.explanation: DNA replication doubles the content from 8 to 16 picograms during S phase.
DNA doubles during S phase, increasing from 8 to 16 picograms.
DNA doubles during S phase, not halves. It increases to 16 picograms.
After mitosis, the 16 picograms is divided equally, giving each daughter cell 8 picograms.
The 16 picograms is split equally between two daughter cells during mitosis.
Each daughter cell receives half of 16, which is 8 picograms, not 4.

toLevel4.question: If the G2 checkpoint is disabled, cells with replication {{blank:1}} could enter mitosis and produce {{blank:2}} daughter cells.

options.text: errors
options.explanation: The G2 checkpoint normally catches replication errors; without it, faulty DNA passes through.

options.text: success
options.explanation: Successful replication is not the concern; the issue is that errors would go undetected.

options.text: delays
options.explanation: The G2 checkpoint checks for accuracy, not timing delays in replication.

options.text: defective
options.explanation: Without error checking, daughter cells would inherit replication mistakes, making them defective.

options.text: identical
options.explanation: Errors in replication would mean daughter cells are not identical to the parent.

options.text: enlarged
options.explanation: The issue is genetic defects, not cell size.

toLevel5.question: A graph shows DNA content per cell over time. There is a plateau at 2n, a rise to 4n, a second plateau, then a drop back to 2n. Which cell cycle events do these sections represent?

options.text: G1 at 2n, S phase rise to 4n, G2 plateau at 4n, and mitosis drop to 2n
options.explanation: DNA stays at 2n in G1, doubles during S, remains at 4n in G2, and returns to 2n after mitotic division.

options.text: S phase at 2n, G1 rise to 4n, mitosis plateau at 4n, and G2 drop to 2n
options.explanation: S phase is the rise, not the plateau at 2n. The sequence is G1, S, G2, M.

options.text: Mitosis at 2n, G2 rise to 4n, G1 plateau at 4n, and S phase drop to 2n
options.explanation: This reverses the order. DNA rises in S phase and drops at mitosis.

options.text: G2 at 2n, mitosis rise to 4n, S phase plateau at 4n, and G1 drop to 2n
options.explanation: DNA rises during S phase (replication), not during mitosis.

toLevel5.question: A researcher compares two cell populations. Population A has most cells with 2n DNA content, while Population B has most cells with 4n DNA content. What can be inferred?

options.text: Population A cells are mostly in G1 or G0, while Population B cells are in G2 or M phase
options.explanation: 2n DNA indicates pre-replication (G1/G0); 4n indicates post-replication (G2/M phase).

options.text: Population A is dividing more rapidly than Population B based on the DNA content
options.explanation: Having 2n DNA means most cells have not replicated, suggesting less active division, not more.

options.text: Population B cells have completed division while Population A cells have not started
options.explanation: 4n DNA means replication is complete but division has not yet occurred; 2n could mean division is complete.

options.text: Both populations are in the same phase but have different amounts of total DNA
options.explanation: Different DNA contents indicate different cell cycle phases, not the same phase.

toLevel5.question: Cancer cells often have defective checkpoints. How does this relate to the role of DNA replication as a precursor to division?

options.text: Without functional checkpoints, cells may divide with incompletely or inaccurately replicated DNA
options.explanation: Defective checkpoints allow cells to bypass replication quality control, leading to mutations and genomic instability.

options.text: Defective checkpoints prevent DNA replication from occurring at all in cancer cells
options.explanation: Cancer cells still replicate DNA; the issue is that checkpoints do not verify replication accuracy.

options.text: Cancer cells replicate DNA more accurately because checkpoints slow the process down
options.explanation: Defective checkpoints reduce accuracy, not increase it. Checkpoints ensure quality, not cause slowness.

options.text: Checkpoint defects have no relationship to DNA replication or cell division errors
options.explanation: Checkpoint defects directly relate to replication errors passing into daughter cells.

toLevel5.question: A student argues that DNA replication is not necessary for cell division because some bacteria divide without a formal S phase. What is the flaw in this reasoning?

options.text: Bacteria still replicate their DNA before division; the process differs but the principle is the same
options.explanation: All cells must replicate DNA before dividing. Bacteria replicate during binary fission, which is different from eukaryotic S phase but serves the same purpose.

options.text: The student is entirely correct that some organisms divide without any DNA replication
options.explanation: No organism divides successfully without replicating its DNA first; the mechanism may differ but replication is universal.

options.text: Bacteria do not contain DNA, so the comparison is invalid for this type of analysis
options.explanation: Bacteria contain circular DNA that must be replicated before binary fission.

options.text: Only eukaryotic cells require DNA for cell division to occur at any stage
options.explanation: All cells, prokaryotic and eukaryotic, require DNA replication before division.

toLevel5.question: Flow cytometry data shows three peaks in a cell population: at 2n, between 2n and 4n, and at 4n. What does the middle peak represent?

options.text: Cells currently in S phase, partway through DNA replication
options.explanation: Cells between 2n and 4n are actively replicating DNA, placing them within S phase.

options.text: Cells in G0 that have permanently exited the cell cycle
options.explanation: G0 cells would have 2n DNA content, not an intermediate amount.

options.text: Cells that have completed mitosis and returned to normal levels
options.explanation: Post-mitosis cells return to 2n; intermediate values indicate ongoing replication.

options.text: Cells with damaged DNA that cannot be categorised into a phase
options.explanation: Intermediate DNA content is normal for S phase cells, not an indicator of damage.

toLevel5.question: Why would a chemotherapy drug that targets S phase be effective against rapidly dividing cancer cells but less harmful to non-dividing cells?

options.text: Rapidly dividing cells spend more time in S phase replicating DNA, increasing their exposure to the drug
options.explanation: Cancer cells divide frequently, so they are in S phase more often and are more vulnerable to S-phase-targeting drugs.

options.text: Non-dividing cells do not contain any DNA and are therefore immune to all drug effects
options.explanation: Non-dividing cells contain DNA but are in G0/G1 and not replicating, so S phase drugs do not affect them.

options.text: The drug destroys all cell types equally regardless of their division rate and phase
options.explanation: S phase drugs specifically affect cells undergoing replication, not all cells equally.

options.text: Cancer cells are in G0 phase most of the time, making them vulnerable to S phase drugs
options.explanation: Cancer cells are actively dividing, not in G0. They are vulnerable because they are frequently in S phase.

toLevel5.question: A cell biologist observes that a mutant cell line completes replication in half the normal time but produces many more replication errors. What trade-off does this illustrate?

options.text: Speed of replication versus accuracy, showing that faster copying increases error rate
options.explanation: Faster replication reduces proofreading time, leading to more errors. This shows the trade-off between speed and fidelity.

options.text: Cell size versus DNA content, showing that smaller cells replicate with more precision
options.explanation: The observation is about replication speed and accuracy, not cell size.

options.text: Energy use versus membrane integrity during the replication process in these cells
options.explanation: The trade-off described is between replication speed and accuracy, not energy or membranes.

options.text: Checkpoint frequency versus cell division rate in normal dividing populations
options.explanation: The observation directly shows the speed-accuracy trade-off in DNA replication.

toLevel5.question: Comparing mitosis and meiosis, how does the requirement for DNA replication differ between these two processes?

options.text: Both require replication before division, but meiosis produces cells with half the DNA content
options.explanation: Both processes require S phase replication, but meiosis involves two divisions, resulting in cells with half the original DNA.

options.text: Only mitosis requires DNA replication; meiosis divides without any prior replication
options.explanation: Both mitosis and meiosis require DNA replication during S phase before division begins.

options.text: Only meiosis requires DNA replication; mitosis can proceed without the replication step
options.explanation: Both processes require replication. Mitosis cannot proceed without doubling the DNA first.

options.text: Neither process requires DNA replication because chromosomes split on their own accord
options.explanation: Both mitosis and meiosis require DNA replication to ensure proper chromosome distribution.

toLevel5.question: Flow cytometry data showing peaks at 2n, between 2n and 4n, and at 4n represents cells in {{blank:1}}, {{blank:2}}, and G2/M phase respectively.

options.text: G1/G0
options.explanation: Cells at 2n have not replicated their DNA, placing them in G1 or G0.

options.text: M phase
options.explanation: M phase cells have 4n DNA content, not 2n.

options.text: S phase
options.explanation: S phase cells have intermediate DNA content between 2n and 4n.

options.text: S phase
options.explanation: Cells with DNA content between 2n and 4n are actively replicating during S phase.

options.text: G2 phase
options.explanation: G2 cells have completed replication and would have 4n content.

options.text: G0 phase
options.explanation: G0 cells have exited the cycle and would have 2n content.

toLevel5.question: Chemotherapy drugs targeting S phase are effective against cancer because rapidly dividing cells spend more time {{blank:1}} DNA, making them more {{blank:2}} to the drug.

options.text: replicating
options.explanation: S phase is when DNA replication occurs; rapidly dividing cells are frequently in this phase.

options.text: destroying
options.explanation: S phase involves replication of DNA, not its destruction.

options.text: condensing
options.explanation: Condensation of chromosomes occurs during prophase of mitosis, not during S phase.

options.text: vulnerable
options.explanation: Being in S phase more often increases exposure to the drug, making cancer cells more vulnerable.

options.text: resistant
options.explanation: Frequent S phase entry increases vulnerability, not resistance, to S-phase-targeting drugs.

options.text: dormant
options.explanation: Rapidly dividing cells are active, not dormant. Dormant cells would be in G0.
